newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan police clash with Islamists, 50 injured.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan police clash with Islamists, 50 injured.

text.p: Pakistani police detained leaders of the religious Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) party on Monday amid a second day of chaotic skirmishes with JI protesters in Islamabad and Rawalpindi, in which 50 people were hurt.
Staff of the private Edhi ambulance service said about 35 people had been injured by police baton charges and teargas in Rawalpindi and about 15 in the nearby capital.
Police picked up JI leader Qazi Hussain Ahmed and his deputy Khurshid Ahmed from the latter's house in Islamabad. The party's number three, Ghafoor Ahmed, was detained separately.
"They have no written orders nor any right to arrest me," the JI leader, holding a Koran, told reporters as he was being taken away. "Now there will be a campaign all over the country."
Police also detained Ejaz ul-Haq, son of former military ruler General Mohammad Zia-ul-Haq, state-run media said.

Police fired dozens of tear gas canisters to disperse several hundred JI demonstrators who had managed to get within a few hundred metres (yards) of parliament, where JI had planned to hold a sit-in to protest against what they said was official corruption.
At first police stood by as the Islamic militants knelt to pray, blocking the city's main Jinnah Avenue, but broke up the gathering when organisers announced that the sit-in had begun.
Throughout the day security forces blocked access roads to the capital to prevent demonstrators from reaching parliament.
JI militants fought cat-and-mouse battles with police in the Aabpara district of the capital. They burned tyres and wooden crates as police on rooftops fired teargas to disperse them.
Police hunting for young JI militants searched a mosque and detained several people in the streets, apparently at random.

Demonstrators caught one policeman and beat him, finally letting him run off with his trousers in tatters, but keeping his riot shield. They seized a teargas launcher from another policeman, but could find no ammunition for it.
Several teargas canisters fell among houses in the residential district, where one woman carrying a child rushed in panic out of her house, tears streaming from her eyes.
At least 29 people were injured in similar clashes on Sunday and newspapers said up to 100 had been hurt, none seriously.
"We have come out on the streets to wage jihad (holy war) and bring Islamic revolution in the country," newspapers quoted JI leader Qazi Hussain Ahmed as saying on Sunday.
Cellular telephone services went dead on Monday morning after resuming for a few hours on Sunday. They were cut off on Saturday night, apparently to disrupt JI communications.
Paramilitary troops were brought into the capital to guard parliament, the prime minister's secretariat, the president's house, the foreign ministry and the diplomatic enclave.
Most schools and universities in Islamabad remained closed for a second day and many people did not go to work.
